slides.0.title: Geography and climate
slides.0.subtitle: A patchwork of the Atlantic, the Pyrenees and river valleys
slides.1.title: Extent and sub-regions
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Location
slides.1.highlights.0.content: wein.plus: it lies west of the Massif Central, east of the Atlantic and north of the Pyrenees, covering the Dordogne, Garonne and Adour catchments, and excludes Bordeaux
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Four sub-regions
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Wikipedia lists the Dordogne, Garonne, Gascony (including Béarn) and the northern Basque Country; Wine Folly groups them as Bergerac and Dordogne, Garonne and Tarn, the Lot, and the Pyrénées
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Conflicting area figures
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Wikipedia gives about 16,000 ha, Wine Folly about 120,000 acres and wein.plus about 160,000 ha; they disagree, so area is not tested
slides.1.content: This is not one compact region but a scatter of wine districts.
slides.2.title: An Atlantic-led climate
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Atlantic influence
slides.2.highlights.0.content: wein.plus: humid winters and springs, warm summers and long sunny autumns; Wine Folly: most of the region is Atlantic, with Bergerac slightly warmer
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Shifting east
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Wine Folly: in Garonne and Tarn the west is Atlantic-influenced while the east has a Mediterranean climate with less rain and higher temperatures
slides.2.highlights.2.title: The Autan wind
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Wine With Seth: Gaillac sits between Atlantic and Mediterranean influences with a continental character, hot dry summers and the warm east wind called the Autan
slides.2.content: The further east, the drier and warmer.
slides.3.title: The Pyrenean foothills
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Jurançon's rainfall
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Wine With Seth: an oceanic temperate climate with about 1,200 mm of rain a year and vineyards at 200–600 m
slides.3.highlights.1.title: The foehn
slides.3.highlights.1.content: The warm dry southern foehn aids autumn drying for late harvests (Wine With Seth)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Diurnal variation
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Altitude brings meaningful day-night variation, preserving acidity (Wine With Seth)
slides.3.content: The mountains bring rain, and also the dry wind that shapes the sweet wines.
slides.4.title: Valleys and soils
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Cahors
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Alluvial terraces in the meanders of the Lot, with the limestone Causses plateau above; vineyards sit on the second to fourth terraces at 90–350 m (Wine With Seth, Wikipedia)
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Gaillac's four terroirs
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Left-bank gravelly boulbènes, right-bank clay-limestone Premières Côtes slopes, the Cordes limestone plateau and Cunac acid schists (mainly Gamay)
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Fronton and Jurançon
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Négrette suits boulbènes best (siliceous clay with sand and gravel) (Wine With Seth); Jurançon has poudingue pebbly conglomerate in the northeast and flysch in the south
slides.4.content: A single river or slope is often a terroir of its own.
